claims.text: The starting material is as-received, pre-exposure Q235 mild carbon steel.
Q235 samples will be annealed at 750 °C for 2 hours and then cooled under controlled conditions.
Annealing Q235 at 750 °C for 2 hours reduces grain-boundary defects.
Annealing Q235 at 750 °C for 2 hours reduces residual stresses.
Using an inert atmosphere during annealing minimizes formation of a pre-oxidized surface layer while retaining the annealing-induced microstructural modification.
Reduced grain-boundary defects and residual stresses promote formation of a more uniform, coherent, and adherent oxide scale during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
The in situ oxide scale on annealed Q235 will primarily contain magnetite and hematite sublayers.
A coherent and adherent oxide scale is more resistant to salt-induced dissolution and spallation.
Untreated Q235 has a higher defect density than annealed Q235.
Untreated Q235 forms a porous, poorly adherent oxide scale that is prone to spallation.
Porosity and spallation of the untreated-steel scale result in a higher corrosion rate.
Inert-atmosphere-annealed Q235 will exhibit less mass loss or a smaller adverse mass change than untreated Q235 during exposure to 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl at 700–900 °C.
Inert-atmosphere-annealed Q235 will have a more uniform and adherent oxide scale than untreated Q235 after molten-salt exposure.
Inert-atmosphere-annealed Q235 will exhibit lower corrosion-current density than untreated Q235 in room-temperature 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
Air-annealed Q235 may exhibit improved corrosion performance, but any improvement may be caused partly by its pre-formed oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism applies in both 700–900 °C molten salt and room-temperature aqueous NaCl when oxide-growth kinetics and substrate microstructure determine corrosion behavior.
The mechanism should not be inferred when annealing creates a substantial pre-formed oxide layer that masks the contribution from microstructural modification.
A three-arm comparison of untreated, air-annealed, and inert-atmosphere-annealed Q235 is intended to separate pre-oxidation effects from bulk microstructural effects.
Mass change, SEM/EDS scale morphology, XRD phase identification, and electrochemical current density will be used as corrosion-response measurements.

Failure of inert-atmosphere-annealed samples to show statistically significant improvements, or performance indistinguishable from untreated samples, would falsify the proposed microstructure-only protection mechanism.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires the inert-annealed material to improve relative to untreated Q235 and allows air-annealed Q235 also to improve, whereas the falsification rule can be read as requiring the inert-annealed material to outperform both untreated and air-annealed samples. Equality between the two annealed groups would therefore trigger the rule even if both outperform untreated steel, which would not by itself refute an annealing-induced microstructural effect.
